strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to incorporate strong masking into supervised training: shared network parameters, supervised learning on unmasked inputs, and detached prediction targets for masked inputs. Its practical contribution and supporting experiments favor weak acceptance.

Improvements are consistent across strong ImageNet recipes and model sizes. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points over DeiT-III. The repeated experiments support the central result: Table A.12 reports 84.08±0.02 for ViT-B with MaskSub versus 83.46±0.04 for the baseline.

The paper addresses the additional-computation confound directly. Table 7 reports 84.1% accuracy for ViT-B with MaskSub using 25 GPU-days, versus 83.7% for longer baseline training using 26 GPU-days. Table 8 also shows a favorable accuracy–cost comparison with CoSub.

Evaluation breadth is substantial: multiple architectures, pretrained-model fine-tuning, transfer learning, and additional language and vision-language experiments. The supplement provides relevant vision evidence beyond classification, including ADE20k improvements of 0.4–0.6 mIoU, modest COCO gains, and an ImageNet-A improvement from 36.8% to 41.9% for ViT-B.

The formulation, pseudocode, detailed training recipes, masking-ratio and loss-weight ablations, and selected three-seed experiments support reproducibility. A code URL is provided, although its contents were not verified. Source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-uhaq9_gv/call-ac8052dd3c6b4aafb153deac8bf55b2a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: the method combines existing self-distillation and masking ideas, with its main distinction being their efficient integration into strong supervised recipes. The relationship to GradAug, CoSub, and MaskedKD deserves sharper technical differentiation. Moreover, Table 6 compares different training recipes; it cannot establish the accompanying claim that earlier self-distillation methods are incompatible with modern recipes.

The proposed 'automatic difficulty control' is a plausible interpretation rather than an established mechanism. Aggregate gradient norms in Figure 3 do not demonstrate the claim that masking affects only successfully classified examples; the loss contains no correctness gate. Table A.7 also shows a substantial improvement without masking, from 77.4% to 78.4%, indicating that part of the gain comes from other aspects of the training formulation. Table A.6 should explicitly define the loss used in its 'w/o KD' control.

The general-benefit claims require qualification. In Table 10, adding MaskSub during fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.9% to 89.6% with the same MaskSub-pretrained backbone. Section 4.2 also acknowledges that CLIP fine-tuning achieves the same best accuracy as the baseline; its reported improvement concerns the final checkpoint.

The practical advantage depends on architecture and effect size. Section 4.3 states that hierarchical architectures require approximately twice the training computation, while Swin-T improves by only 0.1 percentage point. Although core ViT experiments include repeated runs, uncertainty is not reported for several small gains, including the 0.1-point BEiTv2 and Swin-T improvements. Uniform claims of significant improvements therefore exceed the evidence.

Minor reporting errors should be corrected separately from the scientific concerns: Table 10 labels the ViT-S Cars change from 80.9% to 92.2% as +1.3 instead of +11.3 points. Section 4.4 claims one-sixth of GradAug's training cost, whereas Table 9's total costs give 8.6/23.4, approximately 0.37. These errors do not overturn the supported empirical contribution.
